chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Company

Super Micro Computer, Inc. (SMCI, NASDAQ) is a San Jose, California–headquartered designer and manufacturer of server platforms, storage systems, and integrated rack-scale AI infrastructure. Co-founder Charles Liang has served as Chairman, Chief Executive Officer, and President since incorporating the business in 1993 — one of the longest founder-CEO continuous tenures in US technology. His wife and co-founder Sara Liu continues as Senior Vice President; CFO David Weigand has held the position since 2020. Manufacturing spans substantial operations in Taiwan and the San Jose base.

The core technology franchise is the Datacenter Building Block Solutions (DCBBS) platform — a modular architecture allowing Super Micro to configure and ship novel server designs faster than integrated competitors when a new silicon generation arrives. That capability proved decisive as Nvidia's H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families each demanded bespoke thermal, power, and interconnect designs on compressed roadmap cycles.

## The AI Revenue Inflection

Super Micro's fiscal year ends in June. Through fiscal 2022, revenues stood at $5.20 billion; fiscal 2023 grew 37 percent to $7.12 billion. Fiscal 2024 then produced one of the steepest single-year revenue scaling events in US enterprise server history: [$14.94 billion](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2025/Supermicro-Announces-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx), more than doubling the prior year, as hyperscaler and AI cloud customers — including CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, and Nebius — absorbed GPU-equipped cluster platforms at a rate that outpaced most internal planning assumptions.

| Fiscal Year (ending June) | Revenue | YoY |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $5.20B | — |
| FY2023 | $7.12B | +37% |
| FY2024 | $14.94B | +110% |
| FY2025 | $22.0B | +47% |
| FY2026 YTD (9 months, Mar 2026) | $27.9B | — |

*Sources: [ir.supermicro.com FY2025 results](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2025/Supermicro-Announces-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx); [ir.supermicro.com Q3 FY2026](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2026/Supermicro-Announces-Third-Quarter-Fiscal-Year-2026-Financial-Results/default.aspx)*

Fiscal 2025 extended the run to [$22.0 billion](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2025/Supermicro-Announces-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx) — 47 percent growth despite the governance disruption described below — with Liang noting the company had grown "AI solution leadership in Neoclouds, CSPs, Enterprises, and Sovereign entities." In fiscal 2026, quarterly revenue reached $12.7 billion in Q2 (October–December 2025) before pulling back to $10.2 billion in Q3 (January–March 2026), which management attributed to customer-site power and networking readiness delays rather than demand erosion. Full-year FY2026 guidance stands at $38.9–$40.4 billion. AI GPU-related platforms contributed more than 80 percent of Q3 FY2026 revenue.

## The Governance Crisis Arc

The company's ascent was interrupted on August 27, 2024, when [Hindenburg Research](https://hindenburgresearch.com) published a short-seller report alleging accounting manipulation, export-control violations, and related-party irregularities. On October 30, 2024, Ernst & Young resigned as independent registered public accounting firm, citing inability to rely on management representations — a disclosure carrying extraordinary market weight. Nasdaq issued non-compliance notices as the fiscal 2024 10-K remained unfiled.

The board convened an independent special committee. [BDO USA was engaged as successor auditor on November 18, 2024](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2024/Supermicro-Announces-Appointment-of-BDO-USA-as-Independent-Auditor-and-Filing-of-Compliance-Plan-with-Nasdaq/default.aspx). On December 2, the [special committee reported](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2024/Supermicro-Announces-Completion-of-Review-by-Independent-Special-Committee/default.aspx) no evidence of fraud or misconduct by management or the board; 52 sales transactions reviewed for revenue-recognition accuracy found no problematic patterns; no restatements were required. The fiscal 2024 10-K was filed on February 25, 2025 — the final day of the Nasdaq deadline. BDO issued a clean opinion on the financial statements while identifying material weaknesses in internal controls, including IT control gaps and insufficient documentation over manual journal entries, drawing an adverse opinion on internal controls. Nasdaq confirmed compliance was restored the same day.

The governance file remains open. The Department of Justice and Securities and Exchange Commission both issued subpoenas related to the Hindenburg allegations; those investigations were active as of the snapshot date. In March 2026, co-founder and board member Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw was indicted on federal charges of conspiring to divert more than $2.5 billion in Nvidia chip–equipped servers to Chinese buyers in violation of US export controls. Liaw departed the board following the indictment. On the May 2026 earnings call, Liang said "no one" at the company beyond the three indicted individuals was involved.

## Nvidia Partnership and Blackwell

Super Micro's DCBBS architecture produced a measurable time-to-market advantage during the Blackwell GPU transition. In February 2025, the company announced full production availability of more than [30 Nvidia Blackwell–based solutions](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2025/Supermicro-Ramps-Full-Production-of-NVIDIA-Blackwell-Rack-Scale-Solutions-with-NVIDIA-HGX-B200/default.aspx), headlined by the Nvidia GB200 NVL72 SuperCluster — a 48U direct liquid–cooled rack integrating 72 B200 GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs. A partnership with Eviden extended GB200 NVL72 access across European, Indian, Middle Eastern, and South American markets.

> "Supermicro's transformation into a total datacenter infrastructure provider is accelerating. Our margin recovery and the rapid growth of our DCBBS business demonstrate that our business remains robust." — Charles Liang, May 2026

## Central Tension

Super Micro enters the post-restoration period as the principal pure-play AI server franchise in US public markets. The revenue arc from $5.2 billion in FY2022 to a $40 billion forward run rate in FY2026 is without precedent among dedicated server OEMs. Three questions animate what follows: how durable is the AI capex cycle for SMCI specifically against Dell, HPE, and Lenovo platforms carrying deeper enterprise relationships and lower governance risk perception; what does sustainable post-restoration governance look like when internal-control material weaknesses persist, BDO's adverse ICFR opinion has not yet been cured, and federal investigations remain active; and how does the Nvidia partnership — the single largest structural dependency in the revenue base — evolve as hyperscalers develop custom silicon alternatives and Nvidia moves toward Rubin-generation hardware.

---

chapters.title: From 1993 founding through 2018 NASDAQ suspension restoration to the AI inflection
chapters.body:
## The San Jose Foundation, 1993

Charles Liang and his wife Sara Liu incorporated Super Micro Computer in San Jose, California in 1993 with a thesis that has proved more durable than almost any other in the server industry: that modular, configurable server hardware built around standardised components would outperform proprietary architectures as enterprise computing workloads diversified. Liang, an engineer by training, had developed his manufacturing intuitions in the computing systems industry before concluding that the dominant server vendors of the early 1990s were leaving substantial margin and flexibility on the table by locking customers into proprietary configurations.

The founding structure established a pattern that persisted through the subsequent three decades. Liang served simultaneously as Chairman, Chief Executive Officer, and President — a triple-role concentration unusual even by the standards of founder-led technology companies. Liu took on a co-founder and operational role, eventually serving as Senior Vice President and providing the institutional continuity that a fast-moving hardware manufacturer required. The San Jose location placed the company in the centre of the supply chain relationships, customer proximity, and engineering talent that the server business demanded.

Through the 1990s and into the 2000s, Super Micro scaled across enterprise server categories by executing on the modular building block architecture that Liang positioned as the company's core differentiator. Where larger vendors built proprietary stacks, Super Micro offered configurability. Where margin-focused competitors bundled services and software, Super Micro emphasised hardware density and thermal efficiency — characteristics that would acquire new salience as data centre power consumption became a primary operating constraint decades later.

## The 2007 IPO and the Growth Era

Super Micro Computer completed its initial public offering on NASDAQ in March 2007, listing under the ticker SMCI. The IPO gave the company additional capital to scale manufacturing, deepen its Taiwan operations alongside its San Jose base, and invest in the engineering capacity needed to accelerate product cycles. The years following the IPO saw Super Micro expand its customer base across enterprise verticals including financial services, telecommunications, and the emerging cloud infrastructure market, which was beginning to absorb substantial server volume.

The period from 2007 through the mid-2010s established Super Micro as a credible second-tier server franchise competing against Dell, Hewlett-Packard Enterprise, and Lenovo on price-performance while maintaining the flexibility that hyperscaler customers increasingly valued. Revenue scaled steadily, if not spectacularly, during this period as the company deepened relationships with customers who needed customised hardware configurations at volumes that the major vendors found uneconomical to serve.

## The 2018 Suspension and the SEC Settlement

The first major governance rupture in Super Micro's history arrived in 2018, when the company failed to file its annual report on Form 10-K with the Securities and Exchange Commission within the required timeframe. The filing delays, which extended across multiple quarters, triggered a NASDAQ notification process that ultimately resulted in Super Micro shares being suspended from trading on the exchange. The suspension represented the most serious institutional setback in the company's twenty-five-year history to that point, and subjected Liang's stewardship to a degree of external scrutiny that the founder-controlled governance structure had not previously faced.

The accounting and reporting irregularities underlying the filing delays led to an SEC investigation. In August 2020, Super Micro Computer agreed to pay $17.5 million to settle charges brought by the Securities and Exchange Commission related to accounting violations. The SEC's findings covered issues including revenue recognition timing and premature booking of sales. The company neither admitted nor denied the SEC's findings as part of the settlement. Super Micro was relisted on NASDAQ in 2019 after completing the delayed filings and satisfying the exchange's compliance requirements.

The 2018–2019 episode established a precedent that would prove consequential: when governance or reporting concerns surfaced at Super Micro, the pattern of delayed disclosure and eventual institutional resolution would recur. Investors who tracked the company through the 2024 governance events found the earlier episode instructive context.

## Operational Restoration and the AI Inflection, 2019–2023

The years following the NASDAQ relisting were defined by two simultaneous trajectories: the normalisation of Super Micro's reporting and governance framework under continued Liang leadership, and the beginning of what would become one of the most dramatic single-company revenue escalations in US server history.

Liang appointed David Weigand as Chief Financial Officer in 2021, providing the finance function with additional seniority as revenue scale demands on the reporting infrastructure increased. The period from 2019 through 2022 saw Super Micro re-establish its standing with customers who had remained cautious during the suspension period, while simultaneously positioning the company's direct liquid cooling technology and Nvidia GPU integration capabilities for the infrastructure cycle that was beginning to take shape.

The AI inflection arrived with force in fiscal year 2023. Super Micro's revenue for the fiscal year ending June 2023 reached $7.12 billion, up from $5.20 billion in fiscal 2022. Then fiscal year 2024 — the twelve months ending June 2024 — produced a result that had few precedents in enterprise server history: revenue of $14.94 billion, a year-over-year increase of more than 100 percent.

| Fiscal Year (ending June) | Revenue (USD billions) |
|---|---|
| FY2022 | $5.20 |
| FY2023 | $7.12 |
| FY2024 | $14.94 |

The acceleration reflected Super Micro's structural positioning at the intersection of the Nvidia GPU server ecosystem and the hyperscaler and AI cloud customer base that was absorbing capital expenditure at an extraordinary rate. The company's modular building block architecture enabled rapid product cycle execution as Nvidia transitioned through successive GPU generations — H100, H200, and the Blackwell B100 and B200 platforms — without the lengthy re-engineering cycles that competitors with more integrated product lines required. Customers including hyperscaler cloud providers and AI infrastructure operators such as CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, Crusoe, and Nebius absorbed substantial server volume as the AI infrastructure buildout accelerated through calendar 2023 and into 2024.

## The Hindenburg Short and the Auditor Resignation, August–October 2024

On August 27, 2024, Hindenburg Research — the short-selling firm that had previously targeted Nikola, Adani Group, and other high-profile subjects — published a short-seller report on Super Micro Computer. The Hindenburg report alleged accounting and operational concerns at the company, drawing on former employee accounts, supplier relationships, and analysis of Super Micro's financial disclosures. The report alleged potential sanctions evasion, undisclosed related-party transactions, and accounting practices that Hindenburg characterised as raising material questions about the integrity of Super Micro's reported financials.

Super Micro shares fell sharply in the sessions following the report's publication. The company declined to detail responses to the specific allegations beyond noting its intention to demonstrate that the concerns were unfounded. Sophisticated investors who had tracked the 2018 suspension found the Hindenburg allegations particularly resonant given the earlier SEC settlement's findings on revenue recognition.

The situation deteriorated sharply in October 2024 when Ernst & Young, which had served as Super Micro's independent registered public accounting firm, resigned. EY's resignation letter, filed with the SEC, stated that the firm was not in a position to rely on representations of management and the audit committee and cited concerns that had led it to conclude it could no longer serve as the company's auditor. The resignation of a Big Four auditor mid-engagement, without completion of the annual audit, represented an extreme and rare corporate event. SMCI shares fell to levels not seen since the pre-AI-inflection period.

The company announced in November 2024 that it had engaged BDO USA as its successor independent registered public accounting firm. BDO, a large national accounting firm with substantial public company audit experience, took on the responsibility of completing the delayed annual audit and restoring the reporting framework that EY's departure had disrupted.

## The Special Committee Findings, February 2025

Super Micro's board had formed a special committee of independent directors to conduct an internal investigation into the concerns raised by the Hindenburg report and the EY resignation. The special committee, which engaged independent legal counsel and forensic accounting advisers, conducted an investigation that ran through the final months of 2024 and into early 2025.

In February 2025, the special committee delivered its findings. The committee concluded that it had found no evidence of fraud and no evidence of material misstatement in Super Micro's previously reported financial results. The findings represented a significant institutional vindication for Liang and the management team. The special committee did identify internal control weaknesses and governance process improvements that it recommended the company address, and the board additions made through the post-special-committee period — including directors Steve Rieger, Susie Giordano, and Scott Angel — were intended to provide the additional governance independence that the events of 2024 had demonstrated was necessary.

The February 2025 findings, combined with BDO's engagement and the subsequent progress on the delayed 10-K filings, allowed Super Micro to begin the process of returning to normal exchange compliance. For investors who had tracked the company across both the 2018 suspension and the 2024 Hindenburg episode, the pattern of governance rupture followed by institutional resolution — with Liang's operational leadership and the core AI server franchise intact throughout — had now repeated twice across three decades of continuous founder control.

chapters.title: AI server platforms, Building Block, liquid cooling, and customer segments
chapters.body:
## AI Server Platforms: The Nvidia Ecosystem

Super Micro Computer's ascent from a $5.20 billion revenue business in fiscal 2022 to a $14.94 billion franchise by fiscal 2024 — the year ending June 2024 — was not principally a story of market share taken from Dell or Hewlett Packard Enterprise through price competition. It was a story of platform positioning. When Nvidia's HGX H100 GPU complex emerged as the dominant substrate for large-language model training and inference, Super Micro was already embedded in the supply chain with GPU-optimized server designs, a long-standing Nvidia partnership, and the manufacturing agility to convert that positioning into volume faster than most peers.

The company's AI server portfolio is organized around Nvidia's successive GPU generations. The SYS-821GE-TNHR and related HGX H100 SXM5 systems — eight-way GPU nodes drawing up to 10.2 kilowatts of thermal load per chassis — represented the first major wave. As Nvidia transitioned the data center roadmap to H200, which replaces HBM3 memory with HBM3e and lifts per-GPU memory bandwidth from approximately 3.35 terabytes per second to 4.8 terabytes per second, Super Micro introduced corresponding HGX H200 platforms with the same chassis lineage. The mechanical and power-delivery continuity between generations is not incidental: it reflects a deliberate product philosophy that Super Micro calls its Building Block Architecture, described in the company's annual filings with the SEC ([CIK 0000949486](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000949486&type=10-K)) as the ability to mix and match components — motherboards, chassis, power supplies, cooling subsystems — across product lines to reduce time-to-market for new GPU platforms.

The Blackwell generation elevated the engineering stakes materially. Nvidia's GB200 NVL72 configuration — 36 Grace CPUs paired with 72 Blackwell B200 GPUs on a rack-scale NVLink interconnect — requires a full rack solution rather than a conventional tower-and-cable deployment. Super Micro built rack-scale infrastructure for GB200 NVL72 deployments, integrating the NVLink spine, power shelves, and cooling manifolds into a single deliverable. The MGX platform, Nvidia's modular-chassis reference architecture for accelerated computing, further expanded the addressable product space: Super Micro became one of the principal system builders certifying MGX-compliant designs for inference-optimized deployments using L40S and subsequent Nvidia accelerators targeted at enterprise workloads.

## Building Block Architecture

The Building Block Architecture — detailed in the IP & R&D chapter — compresses product development cycles through modular component hierarchies. When Nvidia accelerated GPU roadmap cadence, Super Micro's modular inheritance meant validated chassis and power infrastructure could be adapted rapidly. Charles Liang referenced the architecture directly on the company's fiscal third quarter 2024 earnings call:

> "Our Building Block solution enables us to bring new products to market very quickly. When Nvidia introduces a new GPU, we can have a complete system ready in weeks."

The company does not publish explicit segment revenue broken down by platform generation. The 10-K filing for fiscal year 2024 discloses revenue by product category — server and storage systems versus subsystems and accessories — rather than by GPU platform. Server and storage systems constituted the substantial majority of the $14.94 billion total, with subsystems and accessories representing the remainder. The practical implication is that the AI server platforms, encompassing HGX and MGX configurations for Nvidia GPU workloads, accounted for the preponderance of revenue growth, given the near-doubling of total revenue between fiscal 2023 ($7.12 billion) and fiscal 2024 ($14.94 billion).

The sequential doubling from $7.12 billion to $14.94 billion in fiscal 2024 was driven almost entirely by AI GPU server volume.

## Direct Liquid Cooling

## Direct Liquid Cooling

Direct liquid cooling (DLC) is Super Micro's most consequential near-term infrastructure bet. Conventional air-cooled data center design was engineered for approximately 5 to 15 kilowatts per rack. An eight-way HGX H100 node can approach 100 kilowatts of thermal load — beyond what air cooling can efficiently manage.

Super Micro's DLC systems route chilled liquid — typically water in a closed loop with facility-level heat exchangers — directly to cold plates bonded to GPU packages, CPU packages, and VRM components. The thermal conductivity of water is approximately 25 times that of air. The company has developed DLC solutions for HGX H100, HGX H200, and GB200 NVL72 platforms where liquid cooling is effectively mandatory given the thermal envelope.

The company captures revenue not only from the server itself but from cooling infrastructure — manifolds, quick-disconnect couplings, facility-side heat exchangers, and management software. In investor communications, Super Micro has described liquid-cooled backlog growing faster than air-cooled configurations.

## General-Purpose Tiers: Intel, AMD, Storage, and Edge

AI server platforms, however visible, are layered on top of a general-purpose server portfolio that has been Super Micro's commercial foundation since the 1990s. The company builds X13 and X14 generation motherboard platforms around Intel Xeon Scalable processors — fifth-generation "Emerald Rapids" and successor architectures — as well as AMD EPYC Genoa and Bergamo platforms for cloud-native and memory-bandwidth-intensive workloads. These general-purpose configurations serve enterprise data centers, financial services firms, telecommunications infrastructure, and mid-market IT deployments that are buying compute cycles, storage IOPS, and network throughput rather than GPU-hours.

Storage systems — disaggregated JBODs, all-flash arrays, and object storage nodes — represent a separate product line that Super Micro sells both independently and as companion infrastructure to AI clusters. Large-scale AI deployments require checkpoint storage for model weights, training-data staging, and inference-result logging, creating a natural attach-rate opportunity for Super Micro's storage platforms. Networking components, including high-speed Ethernet switches and InfiniBand-compatible network infrastructure, extend the portfolio further into the rack-level bill of materials.

Edge computing and telecommunications infrastructure represent smaller revenue categories, comprising ruggedized and compact form-factor systems for telecommunications network functions, industrial automation, and edge inference. These segments do not carry the same growth trajectory as AI server platforms but contribute to the company's hardware diversification and broaden its commercial relationships into vertical markets adjacent to the core data center business.

## Customer Segments

Super Micro's customer base, as described in its annual report disclosures, divides broadly into four categories: hyperscaler cloud providers, AI-focused cloud infrastructure operators, enterprise end-users, and high-performance computing institutions including national laboratories.

Hyperscaler relationships — with the principal cloud providers running large-scale GPU training and inference infrastructure — account for a substantial share of AI server revenue. Super Micro does not name hyperscaler customers in routine filings, but the volume concentration implied by the fiscal 2024 revenue profile is consistent with significant hyperscaler exposure. These customers purchase in bulk, often through direct procurement relationships with negotiated pricing and delivery schedules tied to GPU allocation from Nvidia.

AI cloud providers — CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, Crusoe Energy, and Nebius among them — represent a second category that expanded rapidly alongside the GPU capacity buildout of 2023 and 2024. CoreWeave, which disclosed Super Micro as a key server supplier in its IPO filings, exemplifies the pattern: a purpose-built AI cloud that leases GPU capacity to model developers and research institutions, requiring dense GPU clusters delivered on accelerated timelines. These customers value Super Micro's ability to turn configured systems quickly and integrate liquid cooling infrastructure as a single-vendor solution.

Enterprise customers — across financial services, healthcare systems, manufacturing, and telecommunications — represent the broad middle of the market. They buy smaller quantities per transaction but in aggregate contribute meaningfully to general-purpose platform revenue. Their buying cycles are slower and more procurement-governed, but they are less concentrated and provide revenue stability relative to the hyperscaler relationship, which can fluctuate with capital expenditure cycles.

High-performance computing institutions, including Department of Energy national laboratories and university research facilities, occupy the fourth segment. HPC buyers have historically been Super Micro customers for dense compute nodes and have, in more recent periods, adopted GPU-accelerated configurations for scientific computing workloads that overlap with AI model architectures. These relationships carry lower volume than hyperscaler accounts but often involve extended qualification periods and multi-year deployment programs that create durable revenue streams.

The combined profile — hyperscaler concentration at the top, AI cloud velocity in the middle, enterprise breadth below — reflects a business that scaled through a specific GPU super-cycle while maintaining the diversification necessary to weather shifts in hyperscaler capital expenditure priorities. The durability of that profile, following the governance disruptions of late 2024, constituted one of the central questions entering the post-restoration period.

chapters.title: $14.94B FY2024 revenue and the post-restoration trajectory
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Inflection

In the twelve months ending June 30, 2024, Super Micro Computer reported net revenue of $14.94 billion — a figure that had been $7.12 billion the prior fiscal year and $5.20 billion the year before that. The sequential doubling between fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2024 placed the company in rare territory: few hardware manufacturers in the history of the US technology industry have crossed from seven-billion to fifteen-billion in a single fiscal year. The vector was almost entirely artificial intelligence infrastructure. Hyperscaler cloud customers and the emerging class of AI-cloud independents — CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, Crusoe Energy, Nebius — arrived at SMCI with purchase orders measured in racks, then in data-hall allotments, then in campus-scale commitments. The Nvidia HGX H100 and H200 compute platforms that powered those orders ran through SMCI chassis at a conversion rate the company's modular manufacturing architecture was uniquely equipped to absorb.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD) | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 (ended Jun 2022) | $5.20B | — |
| FY2023 (ended Jun 2023) | $7.12B | +36.9% |
| FY2024 (ended Jun 2024) | $14.94B | +109.8% |

The compound growth between FY2022 and FY2024 was approximately 69% annually. Charles Liang, who has served as chairman, chief executive, and president without interruption since co-founding the company in San Jose in 1993, framed the moment on the fiscal fourth-quarter 2024 earnings call in terms of infrastructure readiness:

> "Super Micro is uniquely positioned — with our green computing, our liquid cooling, and our modular architecture — to be at the forefront of AI infrastructure globally."

The statement carried strategic precision. SMCI had not arrived at $14.94 billion through a single product refresh cycle. The Modular Building Block Architecture the company had been refining since its earliest server generations gave it an engineering lever that neither Dell Technologies nor Hewlett Packard Enterprise could replicate on equivalent timelines: a shared component library that let the engineering team configure new GPU-dense platforms around successive Nvidia silicon generations — H100, H200, and then Blackwell B100 and B200 — without rebuilding chassis-level tooling. Time-to-market on new Nvidia product introductions had become a durable competitive advantage.

## AI Server Economics

The revenue arithmetic concealed a margin story that rewarded careful reading. AI servers — defined operationally as GPU-accelerated compute nodes built around Nvidia HGX or MGX baseplates — represented a substantial majority of fiscal 2024 revenue by the time the year closed. The shift in product mix was structurally dilutive to gross margin: AI server bill-of-materials is dominated by the GPU itself, which SMCI passes through at thin spread to preserve the customer relationship for the higher-margin direct liquid cooling loops, networking infrastructure, and platform-level service contracts that surround the compute. Gross margin for fiscal 2024 came in at approximately 14.5 to 15 percent of net revenue, below the 17 percent range the company had operated at when AI server volume was a smaller share of the mix. On an absolute dollar basis, gross profit nonetheless reached roughly $2.2 billion, up substantially year-over-year.

Operating leverage on the underlying cost structure was more favourable. Research and development expense, though growing in absolute terms as SMCI expanded its liquid cooling and rack-scale systems engineering, scaled below revenue growth. Selling, general, and administrative expense was similarly contained. Operating income for fiscal 2024 reached approximately $1.1 to $1.2 billion, implying an operating margin in the 7 to 8 percent range — below what the company achieved in fiscal 2023 when the mix was less GPU-intensive, but representing a substantial dollar expansion of earnings power.

The economics of direct liquid cooling warrant specific note. SMCI had been investing in rear-door heat exchangers and direct-to-chip liquid loops since before the AI server cycle accelerated. By fiscal 2024, those investments had translated into differentiated product lines that commanded higher attachment of infrastructure services and commanded attention from hyperscalers whose power density requirements — GPU clusters operating at 50 to 70 kilowatts per rack and higher — made air cooling uneconomical. Liquid cooling solutions carried structurally higher service and solution content, and accordingly offered gross margin profiles that partially offset the GPU-passthrough dilution in the broader mix.

## Capital Structure and the Convertible Bet

In February 2024, with the stock trading well above its historical range on AI server demand enthusiasm, SMCI executed a $1.725 billion convertible senior note offering — zero-coupon notes due 2029 — at a conversion price of approximately $795 per share. The transaction was among the largest convertible issuances in the server hardware sector's history and provided immediate liquidity for working capital requirements that had grown alongside the revenue base. AI server fulfilment is capital-intensive: components must be purchased and staged before customers take delivery, and payment cycles from hyperscalers — though reliably honoured — impose cash cycle demands that grow proportionally with the volume.

The zero-coupon structure reflected the capital markets context of February 2024. SMCI shares had climbed sharply through the preceding twelve months as AI server demand became legible to equity investors. The company was willing to accept conversion at $795 — a meaningful premium to the then-prevailing share price at issuance — in exchange for a cost-free five-year funding window. The convertible notes sat within a broader capital structure that also included revolving credit facilities, giving the company a layered liquidity profile appropriate for a manufacturer whose inventory and receivables balances had both expanded substantially as revenue scaled.

The February 2024 convertible offering was notably timed in advance of what would prove to be a turbulent second half of calendar 2024. When Hindenburg Research published its short-seller report on August 27, 2024, alleging accounting irregularities and operational concerns, the stock had already retreated meaningfully from its February highs. The convertible structure remained intact — its 2029 maturity provided a long runway insulated from near-term price volatility — though the governance disruption that followed would test the capital markets relationship in ways the February transaction had not anticipated.

## Governance Storm and Reporting Backlog

The sequence of events between August and November 2024 constituted the most acute governance crisis in SMCI's three decades as a public company. Ernst & Young, which had served as the company's independent registered public accounting firm, resigned in October 2024 — an event without direct precedent in the company's reporting history. EY's resignation letter, disclosed in an 8-K filing with the SEC, cited concerns that it was no longer willing to be associated with the company's financial statements. The disclosure triggered immediate regulatory consequences: SMCI received notice from Nasdaq that it risked delisting if it could not file its annual report on Form 10-K for fiscal year 2024 within the required cure period.

BDO USA was engaged as successor independent auditor in November 2024. The engagement represented a significant undertaking: BDO was required to audit financial statements for a company with $14.94 billion in revenue across a fiscal year that had already closed and for which the predecessor auditor had raised concerns sufficient to prompt resignation. The special committee of independent directors, meanwhile, commissioned its own investigation into the accounting and governance allegations raised by Hindenburg and EY.

The special committee delivered its findings in February 2025. The conclusion was dispositive: the investigation found no evidence of fraud and no material misstatement in the company's financial statements. The findings were delivered against a backdrop of intensive document review and executive interviews, and their scope encompassed the allegations in the Hindenburg report as well as the concerns that had precipitated EY's exit. For shareholders who had watched the stock decline substantially between August and the end of calendar 2024, the committee's findings provided the factual foundation for a reassessment of the governance risk premium the market had attached to the company.

## The Restored Reporting Framework

BDO's completion of the fiscal 2024 audit and the February 2025 10-K filing confirmed the $14.94 billion revenue figure without material revision. BDO issued an unqualified opinion on the financial statements. The 2024–2025 cycle followed a structurally parallel pattern to the 2018 episode: allegation, auditor disruption, internal investigation, clean findings, restored framework.

## Competitive Positioning at the $15 Billion Scale

The fiscal 2024 revenue base placed SMCI in direct comparison with the server divisions of peers that operate far larger overall businesses. Dell Technologies' Infrastructure Solutions Group generated roughly comparable AI server volumes over the equivalent period, but Dell's diversification across client computing, software, and services means the AI server cycle represents a smaller share of its total enterprise. HPE's server business, similarly, sits within a portfolio that includes hybrid cloud software and professional services. SMCI's revenue is more purely server and storage hardware, making it — as of fiscal 2024 — the highest-concentration public play on the AI infrastructure build cycle accessible on a major US exchange.

That concentration is simultaneously the company's principal competitive identity and its principal risk factor. Revenue exposure to Nvidia GPU product cycles, hyperscaler capital expenditure decisions, and AI cloud customer funding conditions are more directly felt in SMCI financials than in any peer of comparable scale. The post-restoration trajectory, as it unfolds through fiscal 2025 and into fiscal 2026, will test whether the company can sustain the operating leverage achieved on the way to $14.94 billion — and whether the governance framework BDO and the special committee restored can support the continuous disclosure requirements that an enterprise of this scale demands.

chapters.title: From FY2024 scaling through the Hindenburg event to BDO restoration
chapters.body:
## The Year Revenue Doubled

The eighteen months from July 2023 through February 2025 compressed extraordinary financial drama. Fiscal 2024 revenue reached $14.94 billion — more than doubling fiscal 2023's $7.12 billion. The acceleration was among the steepest single-year revenue expansions in American enterprise hardware history.

The progression quarter by quarter traced the arrival of Nvidia's H100 graphics processing unit into hyperscaler and AI-cloud data centres at scale. In the first fiscal quarter, ending September 2023, Super Micro posted revenue of approximately $2.12 billion — already meaningfully ahead of the comparable prior-year period, yet only a foretaste of what followed. The second quarter, ending December 2023, reached approximately $3.66 billion — a figure that alone exceeded the entire first half of fiscal 2023 — as AI server backlogs converted to recognised shipments and customer deployments accelerated. Charles Liang told analysts on the second-quarter call that demand for the company's GPU-optimised platforms was "very strong across all customer segments" and that Super Micro's liquid-cooling-ready chassis designs gave it structural advantages as GPU thermal density continued to climb.

The third quarter, ending March 2024, produced revenue of approximately $3.85 billion, as the H100 ramp settled at volume and H200 configurations began to appear in forward customer roadmaps. Liang characterised the Building Block Architecture on analyst calls as "the key to why we can bring new products to market so quickly." Chief Financial Officer David Weigand noted in the same period that gross margins reflected the cost pressures of sourcing GPU components at scale but that operating leverage from volume was broadly constructive.

The fourth fiscal quarter, ending June 2024, was the largest in the company's history: revenue of approximately $5.31 billion capped a fiscal year that Super Micro subsequently reported at $14.94 billion in total. The stock, which had begun fiscal 2024 in the mid-two-hundred-dollar range on a pre-split basis, exceeded $1,200 by March 2024. The market was pricing Super Micro as the principal infrastructure beneficiary of the AI capital-expenditure cycle — a direct-play data-centre supplier to companies building large-language-model training and inference clusters.

## The Governance Crisis Arc

On August 27, 2024, Hindenburg Research published a short-seller report targeting Super Micro Computer. The report alleged accounting manipulation, undisclosed related-party transactions, and potential export-control violations. The firm noted that several former employees who had departed during the company's earlier accounting difficulties — which had culminated in a [$17.5 million SEC settlement in August 2020](https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2020-192) — had subsequently been rehired.

The market reaction was swift. Super Micro's stock fell approximately 26 percent over the sessions immediately following publication. The company had not filed its Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended June 2024 by the standard August deadline, citing the need for additional time — a delay that, arriving in the wake of a Hindenburg report, compounded investor unease.

The situation escalated on October 30, 2024, when [Ernst & Young resigned](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1375365/000137536524000142/) as independent auditor. In a letter filed with the SEC, EY stated it had become unwilling to be associated with the financial statements prepared by management. The resignation sent shares down more than thirty percent in a single session. NASDAQ notified the company it risked delisting.

## BDO and the Path to Restoration

In November 2024, [Super Micro engaged BDO USA](https://ir.supermicro.com) as replacement independent auditor. BDO undertook completing the fiscal 2024 audit and reviewing internal controls. The special committee of independent directors concluded its work in February 2025 with unambiguous findings: no evidence of fraud, no evidence of intentional misconduct by management, no material misstatements.

> "The findings confirmed what we have always believed — that Super Micro's management team has acted with integrity." — Charles Liang

Weigand noted the company expected to file the delayed 10-K and become current on all outstanding periodic reports.

## Revenue in Context

The governance events did not impair the structural position — customer relationships that produced $14.94 billion remained operational throughout. The hyperscalers — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta — had each committed to multi-year capital expenditure programmes exceeding fifty billion dollars annually. Super Micro sat structurally close to the Nvidia GPU supply chain in a way few competitors could match.

What the events temporarily impaired was investor confidence in the financial reporting architecture. That confidence began to recover once the special committee findings were published and the audit path restored. The founder who had built Super Micro from a San Jose machine shop in 1993 remained, through all of it, in operational command.

chapters.title: Liang, Liu, Weigand, and the post-special-committee board
chapters.body:
Super Micro Computer has always been, structurally and operationally, a founder's company. When Charles Liang incorporated the business in San Jose in August 1993 — the same summer Intel launched the Pentium — he took three roles simultaneously: chief executive, president, and chairman of the board. Thirty-one years later, through an IPO, a NASDAQ delisting, a federal securities settlement, and the most public governance crisis in the company's history, Liang still held all three. The triple-title structure is not an administrative formality; it is the operating architecture of the enterprise.

## Charles Liang: The Founder Still at the Controls

Liang was born in Chiayi, a mid-sized city on Taiwan's western coastal plain. He took a degree in electrical engineering from the National Taiwan University of Science and Technology, then pursued graduate work at the University of Texas at Arlington, where he earned a master's in electrical engineering. After a stint at Micro Center Computer — a motherboard design and manufacturing firm where he served as president and chief design engineer from July 1991 — Liang made the leap that defined the rest of his professional life, co-founding Super Micro Computer with his wife Chiu-Chu "Sara" Liu in August 1993.

The founding model — modular, configurable server hardware built around vertical integration — became the Building Block Architecture detailed in the IP & R&D chapter. The company's first structural test came in 2018 with NASDAQ delisting and an eventual $17.5 million SEC settlement — detailed in the Corporate History chapter. Forbes named Liang among the 25 most successful Americans of Chinese descent; by early 2024, his equity stake was valued at approximately $3.3 billion.

The 2024–2025 governance crisis — detailed in the News & Catalysts chapter — tested Liang on different dimensions. Through the Hindenburg report, EY resignation, and BDO transition, Liang remained the company's public face with measured posture, maintaining the operational cadence that had driven FY2024 revenue to $14.94 billion.

## Sara Liu: Co-Founder and Institutional Memory

Chiu-Chu "Sara" Liu co-founded Super Micro Computer alongside Liang in 1993, holding a treasurer function in the earliest years of the business. Her formal title has evolved over the company's history; as of the frozen snapshot date she holds the title of Senior Vice President. The co-founder partnership between Liang and Liu — spouses as well as business collaborators — has persisted as one of the structural constants of the company's three-decade run. Liu does not carry a public profile commensurate with her governance role, but the institutional-memory function her continuity provides is not separable from the company's operational DNA, particularly in its manufacturing relationships with Taiwan-based supply chain partners where the founders' shared background carries practical weight.

## David Weigand: Chief Financial Officer Through the Storm

David Weigand joined Super Micro Computer in May 2018 as Senior Vice President and Chief Compliance Officer — a function the company needed given the NASDAQ compliance situation it was navigating at the time. In February 2021 he was named Senior Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, and Chief Compliance Officer, succeeding Kevin Bauer in the CFO function.

Weigand's pre-SMCI career was built primarily in finance roles at technology and semiconductor companies. He served as Vice President, Controller at NEC Electronics America from October 2004 through September 2010, then as Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of Renesas Electronics America — the semiconductor business formed from NEC, Hitachi, and Mitsubishi Electric's semiconductor units — from October 2010 through April 2013. A stint as Vice President, Tax at Silicon Graphics International followed, ending in November 2016 when SGI was acquired by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, where Weigand served as Vice President through April 2018. He holds a B.S. in Accounting from San Jose State University, an M.S. in Taxation from the University of Hartford, and holds California CPA credentials in inactive status.

Weigand's tenure as CFO spanned the sharpest growth period in the company's history — from the early AI infrastructure cycle build-out through the fiscal 2024 peak — and then the governance turbulence of the Hindenburg-to-BDO transition. The special committee's February 2025 findings explicitly found no fraud or misconduct on Weigand's part. However, the report documented "lapses" connected to the rehiring of nine individuals who had previously resigned in 2018 following an earlier audit-related investigation; the committee recommended that the board approve a transition to a new CFO. The board accepted that recommendation and stated it would begin a search "immediately." As of the frozen snapshot date, Weigand remained in the role, with the search extending well into fiscal 2026 — a timeline that raised questions about the board's execution of its own governance commitments.

## The Board: From Governance Gap to Governance Reset

The pre-crisis board carried long tenure and limited independent financial-reporting depth. The departures and additions around the 2024–2025 events reset that composition materially.

**Sherman Tuan** has served as an independent director since February 2007, one of the longest-tenured members of the board. He is founder and CEO of PurpleComm Inc., the connected-television platform operating as 9x9.tv, and was co-founder, President, and CEO of AboveNet Communications from 1996 through 2002. His degree in electrical engineering is from Feng-Chia University in Taiwan. Tuan's tenure predates the IPO; he carries a historical continuity function on the board that is distinct from the post-crisis additions.

**Tally Liu** has served as an independent director since January 2019, joining during the post-relisting reconstruction period. Liu retired in 2015 after serving as CEO of Wintec Industries, a supply chain solutions company for high-technology manufacturers, from 2012 to 2015. Before that he was Chairman and CEO of Newegg Inc., the consumer electronics retailer, from 2008 to 2010. He held VP roles at Knight Ridder. Liu's credentials include a BA in Commerce from National Chengchi University in Taipei, an MBA from Florida Atlantic University, completion of both the Stanford Advanced Finance Program (1986) and Harvard Business School's Advanced Management Program (1998), and holds CISA and CISM certifications. He sits on the Audit Committee.

**Daniel Fairfax** joined the board in July 2019 and brings the most direct CFO-track experience of the independent directors. He served as Senior Vice President and CFO of Brocade Communications from June 2011 through November 2017, having previously held VP roles in operations and services at the same firm. Earlier he was CFO of Foundry Networks from January 2007 through December 2008, and held executive financial management roles at a succession of Silicon Valley technology companies. Fairfax began his career in the National Telecommunications Practice Group at Ernst & Young — a biographical detail that carries some irony given EY's October 2024 resignation. He holds an MBA from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, a BA in Economics from Whitman College, and holds a California CPA credential in inactive status.

**Judy Lin** joined in April 2022, bringing operations and manufacturing depth from the disk drive industry. She spent thirty years in that sector, most recently as Vice President of Western Digital Media Operations from 2007 through her retirement in 2012. Before Western Digital she held VP-level roles at Komag Inc., the thin-film disk supplier, from 1994 through the Western Digital acquisition of Komag in 2007, and prior to that spent eleven years as a Senior Scientist at IBM's Almaden Research Center Storage Systems Division. Lin holds an MSc in Materials Science and Mineral Engineering from the University of California Berkeley and a BS in Chemical Engineering from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan; she also serves as an independent board director of MORESCO Corporation, the Japanese specialty chemicals manufacturer, since 2014.

**Robert Blair** joined in December 2022, also bringing direct operational experience in the semiconductor sector. He served as President and CEO of ESS Technology — a fabless semiconductor company — for nineteen years from September 1999 through July 2018, and as director of that company through August 2019. ESS Technology has a notable connection to the board's broader network: Fred Chan, who served as a Supermicro director from October 2020 until his resignation in March 2024, had himself been a founder and longtime executive of the same company.

**Susie Giordano** joined the board on August 19, 2024 — eight days before the Hindenburg report was published, in timing that would prove unexpectedly apt. Appointed as a Class III director, Giordano brings over twenty-five years of experience advising executive management and boards on governance, compliance, financial reporting, crisis management, and M&A. She spent approximately eleven years at Intel, most recently as interim General Counsel and, separately, as Vice President and Managing Director of Intel Capital. She also served as President and CEO of Deal Fusion, an M&A legal consulting firm, spent five years at Sun Microsystems as Director of M&A and Strategic Investments, served as General Counsel at Aeris IoT SaaS, and began her career at Gunderson Dettmer and Brobeck Phleger & Harrison. She holds a JD from the University of San Francisco School of Law and a BA in Political Science from California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo.

> "Susie has decades of extensive executive management experience leading both internal and external functions for several large technology companies," Liang said at the time of her appointment.

**Scott Angel** was appointed as a Class II director effective March 31, 2025, the most recent addition to the board as of the frozen snapshot date and the most directly connected to the audit remediation process. Angel spent over thirty-seven years in the audit and assurance practice at Deloitte & Touche, including twenty-five years as an audit partner in Silicon Valley. From 1993 until his retirement in December 2017, he led Deloitte's semiconductor industry practice, building deep familiarity with the specific financial reporting and internal control environments of technology hardware companies. He is a member of the AICPA, holds a CPA credential in inactive status, and earned a BA in Business Administration from the University of Washington.

> "We look forward to benefitting from Scott's valuable insights and fresh perspectives on our Board as we work together to advance our vision for Supermicro's future," Liang said at Angel's appointment.

The board also welcomed Yitai Hu as General Counsel and Senior Vice President, Corporate Development, announced concurrently with Angel's appointment. Hu brought nearly three decades of legal experience from AmLaw 50 firms including Norton Rose Fulbright, Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati, Alston & Bird, and Akin Gump, with expertise spanning intellectual property litigation, corporate governance, and M&A.

## Post-Special-Committee Governance Framework

The February 2025 special committee review — conducted by outside counsel Cooley LLP with forensic accounting support from Secretariat Advisors — produced a clean finding on the core question: no fraud, no material misstatement, no misconduct by management or the board, no expected restatement. Kenneth Cheung was appointed Chief Accounting Officer as an immediate structural response. The CFO search was announced. BDO USA, engaged as auditor in November 2024, provided the accounting continuity the company needed to file its delayed FY2024 10-K, its first-quarter FY2025 10-Q, and its second-quarter FY2025 10-Q, bringing the company back into NASDAQ compliance by February 2025.

The resulting board contains a founder-chairman-CEO whose operational control is structurally undiminished, a CFO whose replacement the board itself endorsed but had not executed by the frozen snapshot date, and a materially strengthened independent director slate with deep audit, legal, and technology-operations credentials. Whether the governance architecture assembled through the 2024–2025 crisis is structurally durable — or whether it represents a crisis-period enhancement that will soften as the memory of the Hindenburg period fades — is the open question the post-special-committee board will answer over the years ahead.

chapters.title: Hyperscalers, AI cloud, Nvidia, and the Taiwan-anchored supply chain
chapters.body:
The fiscal 2024 revenue expansion to $14.94 billion concentrated in a narrowing customer pyramid of hyperscaler cloud providers and pure-play AI cloud operators whose appetite for GPU-dense compute reshaped the global server market.

## The Hyperscaler Core

Super Micro does not name its largest customers in most investor communications, a practice standard among integrated systems suppliers serving competing cloud platforms simultaneously. Its annual filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission ([CIK 0000949486](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000949486)) disclose only when individual customers represent more than ten percent of consolidated net revenues — a threshold that in recent fiscal years has been crossed by a small number of accounts described collectively as "hyperscaler cloud providers." The volume implications of that concentration became legible in the revenue trajectory itself: revenues that had grown steadily through fiscal 2022 and 2023 then lurched upward by more than $7.8 billion in a single fiscal year as hyperscaler AI capital expenditure accelerated.

The structural appeal rests on component-level modularity and manufacturing velocity. The Modular Building Block Architecture allows hyperscalers to iterate through GPU generations without re-engineering chassis or cooling infrastructure. Super Micro's ability to compress the design-to-delivery cycle faster than Dell, HPE, or Lenovo formed the core of its fiscal 2024 revenue story.

## The AI Cloud Tier

Alongside the large hyperscalers, a second customer tier emerged during the fiscal 2023–2024 period that proved equally consequential for Super Micro's revenue scaling: the pure-play AI cloud operators. CoreWeave, the GPU cloud provider that began as a cryptocurrency miner before pivoting to Nvidia GPU infrastructure in 2019, became one of the most visible of these buyers. By the time CoreWeave filed for its initial public offering in early 2025, its prospectus documented the scale of its Nvidia-GPU-based infrastructure investments — a substantial portion of which flowed through Super Micro-assembled HGX server platforms — and the company's dependence on a small number of AI infrastructure suppliers.

Lambda Labs, which operates a cloud platform oriented toward AI research teams and enterprise machine-learning workloads, similarly concentrated procurement toward SMCI-assembled H100 and H200 systems during the peak of the Hopper generation buildout. Crusoe Energy, which had built its initial business model around capturing flared natural gas to power cryptocurrency mining, had by 2024 reoriented toward AI cloud infrastructure with an environmental differentiation thesis, constructing GPU-dense data centers in locations with stranded or renewable power and sourcing server platforms from Super Micro. Nebius Group — the European successor entity formed from the non-Russian assets of Yandex following the conglomerate's restructuring after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — emerged as another buyer as it sought to establish a western AI cloud presence. These names collectively represent a customer segment that, unlike the established hyperscalers, was scaling from near zero, making its procurement decisions highly responsive to delivery timelines and system integration quality rather than entrenched supplier relationships.

## Nvidia: The Keystone Relationship

Super Micro is among a small number of companies worldwide authorized to build systems incorporating Nvidia's HGX baseboards — the multi-GPU compute substrates forming the core of H100, H200, and Blackwell-generation platforms. Nvidia's own DGX systems represent the first-party offering; HGX-based systems from authorized partners constitute the broader commercial market. Being among the first to qualify and ship each new HGX generation has historically translated into a first-mover revenue window.

The dependency is bilateral but asymmetric: Nvidia supplies GPU silicon for which no alternative vendor exists; Super Micro provides manufacturing scale and integration expertise that Nvidia's own DGX operations cannot fully absorb during peak demand. [Super Micro investor relations](https://ir.supermicro.com) materials highlight liquid cooling as a key differentiator. The competitive dynamics of this partnership are detailed in the Competitive Position chapter.

## CPU and Memory Supply Chain

Super Micro platforms support both Intel Xeon Scalable processors and AMD EPYC processors, giving hyperscaler and enterprise customers optionality across the two dominant x86 server CPU architectures. Intel has historically held the larger share of Super Micro's CPU-side procurement, reflecting Xeon's entrenched position in enterprise and cloud deployments, but AMD's EPYC family captured meaningful ground in cloud-oriented configurations where core density and memory bandwidth per dollar matter more than Intel's platform ecosystem advantages. The competitive tension between the two CPU vendors has not meaningfully disrupted Super Micro's supply chain; both companies maintain the deep integrator relationships that allow systems qualification to proceed in parallel.

Memory supply presents a more concentrated picture. High Bandwidth Memory — the stacked DRAM architecture integrated directly into Nvidia's H100, H200, and Blackwell GPUs — is produced by a small number of vendors.

| HBM supplier | Generation relevance | Market position |
|---|---|---|
| SK Hynix | HBM3, HBM3E (H100, H200, GB200) | Leading share through Hopper/Blackwell transition |
| Samsung | HBM3E expansion | Active capacity investment, pursuing Blackwell supply |
| Micron | HBM3E (entered market) | Third source, meaningful for supply diversification |

SK Hynix held the leading position in HBM3 and HBM3E supply through the Hopper and early Blackwell generations; Samsung pursued capacity expansion aggressively; Micron's entry into the HBM3E market provided Nvidia — and by extension the AI server supply chain — with a degree of vendor diversification it had lacked during the H100 period. For Super Micro, HBM procurement is structurally indirect: the memory is embedded in Nvidia's GPUs before shipment, but the tightness of HBM supply in 2023 and 2024 constrained overall GPU availability and consequently shaped the revenue cadence of the entire AI server industry. Standard DRAM and NAND, procured separately for system memory and storage, draw from the same Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron supply base that serves the broader enterprise server market.

## The Taiwan Manufacturing Anchor

Super Micro's manufacturing divides across San Jose, California (headquarters, US-facing assembly) and Bade, Taoyuan, Taiwan (high-volume production, supply chain integration). Taiwan hosts the PCB fabricators, stampers, and contract assemblers forming the extended sub-component layer. Proximity to that ecosystem enables the rapid product iteration central to winning first-mover windows on new GPU generations.

## Geopolitical Exposure

That same geographic concentration constitutes the company's most structurally difficult long-term risk. Cross-strait tensions between the People's Republic of China and Taiwan have not receded during the period covered by this dossier. A military confrontation affecting Taiwan would disrupt not only Super Micro's assembly capacity but the broader semiconductor and electronics manufacturing ecosystem — including TSMC's foundry operations that produce Nvidia's GPU silicon — on which the entire AI server supply chain depends. In this sense, Super Micro's geopolitical exposure is less idiosyncratic than it is representative: virtually every GPU-intensive AI infrastructure provider faces the same foundational dependency on Taiwan-based manufacturing, and SMCI's position amplifies that shared exposure by layering its own assembly operations on top of the upstream semiconductor concentration.

US export controls on advanced AI accelerators have reshaped the customer landscape in a separate dimension. Nvidia's H100, A100, and their successors became subject to progressively tightened export restrictions to China and other controlled destinations, limiting Super Micro's addressable market in what might otherwise have been a significant revenue geography. The company's disclosed customer base is weighted heavily toward North American and European buyers; the policy environment has reinforced that concentration rather than allowing the geographic diversification that characterized Super Micro's enterprise business in earlier years. Whether the export control framework represents a competitive constraint shared equally across the industry or a structural floor beneath which no AI server supplier can operate in China without a purpose-downgraded product — Nvidia's H20, for instance — depends on policy trajectories that fall beyond the frozen window of this account.

chapters.title: Where SMCI sits against Dell, HPE, Lenovo, and the Taiwan ODMs
chapters.body:
The AI server market arrived in force during fiscal 2024. Super Micro's $14.94 billion revenue placed it among server-industry heavyweights while remaining something those heavyweights cannot easily replicate: a pure-play AI server franchise focused on platform density, thermal efficiency, and speed to market.

## Dell Technologies: Scale Without Focus

Dell Technologies entered the AI server cycle with structural advantages that Super Micro simply does not possess: a global enterprise sales force measured in tens of thousands of account representatives, decades of institutional relationships, and a financial-services arm that can bundle hardware with leasing and managed services. Dell's Infrastructure Solutions Group — encompassing servers, networking, and storage — generated revenue at a scale that dwarfs Super Micro's top line even in Super Micro's best year, with Dell's consolidated annual revenue running well above $90 billion through fiscal 2024.

Yet Dell's AI server ambitions arrived with the friction characteristic of a diversified franchise sprinting in a narrow lane. Its PowerEdge XE9680 reached customers through traditional enterprise sales motion: multi-quarter procurement cycles and service-contract bundling that AI cloud-native customers view as overhead. Dell's customer mix tilted toward enterprise and government accounts rather than the AI cloud providers placing volume orders at Super Micro.

Dell also carries the architecture of a company that assembles servers from industry-standard components rather than redesigning chassis and thermal systems from first principles at each platform generation. When Nvidia released production HGX H200 configurations, Super Micro was among the first OEMs to ship a validated system at scale. Dell followed on its own integration timeline. The gap, measured in weeks rather than quarters, nonetheless matters in a market where AI infrastructure operators are racing to bring GPU clusters online ahead of competitors.

## HPE: Breadth as Both Asset and Liability

Hewlett Packard Enterprise presents a different competitive texture. HPE's portfolio runs from ProLiant commodity servers through Cray supercomputing systems to GreenLake, its as-a-service cloud management layer. That breadth gives HPE credible presence in HPC and national-laboratory workloads that Super Micro addresses primarily as a hardware supplier. The Frontier system at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Aurora at Argonne both incorporated HPE Cray hardware — a category of landmark government contract that Super Micro has not pursued at that architectural scale.

For commercial AI deployments, however, HPE's portfolio breadth functions as a liability. The GreenLake services wrapper adds margin and stickiness for enterprise customers but introduces procurement complexity that AI cloud providers, optimizing for raw compute cost per GPU-hour, tend to circumvent. HPE's consolidated annual revenue through fiscal 2024 ran at roughly $30 billion — meaningful scale, but a company whose server hardware margin structure is burdened by service-contract obligations and a sprawling product catalogue differing fundamentally from Super Micro's build-to-ship economics.

Where HPE competes most directly with Super Micro is in the liquid-cooled AI cluster segment. HPE's direct liquid cooling offerings for the ProLiant DL380 Gen11 and related platforms address the same thermal density problem that Super Micro's direct liquid cooling systems tackle. But Super Micro reached volume production on high-density liquid-cooled AI racks earlier in the Hopper GPU cycle, and its ability to iterate chassis designs between Nvidia platform generations — Ampere to Hopper to Blackwell — faster than HPE's engineering calendar translated into a recurring early-mover advantage at the accounts where deployment speed is a vendor-selection criterion.

## Lenovo: Global Scale, China Anchor

Lenovo's Infrastructure Solutions Group grew steadily into a globally significant server franchise through the early 2020s — top-three by unit volume in several IDC periods — supported by a manufacturing and distribution footprint spanning China, Hungary, and the Americas. Lenovo's China exposure is a genuine competitive differentiator in the domestic market, where Western OEMs face regulatory friction and procurement-preference headwinds that Lenovo does not. But that same China anchor constrains Lenovo's positioning with US hyperscalers and AI cloud providers navigating export-control compliance, particularly after the Commerce Department tightened advanced AI chip export restrictions through 2023 and 2024.

For the North American and European AI server build-out that drove Super Micro's revenue surge, Lenovo remained a secondary presence. Its ThinkSystem SR670 V3 and SR675 V3 platforms address the GPU-dense workload segment, but Lenovo's go-to-market in the United States has historically leaned on channel partners and system integrators rather than the direct hyperscaler and AI cloud relationships that Super Micro cultivated through Silicon Valley proximity and Liang's longstanding presence in the Nvidia ecosystem.

## The Taiwan ODMs: The Invisible Giants

The competitive dimension that traditional industry analysis most consistently underweights is the Taiwan ODM tier: Quanta Computer, Wiwynn, Inventec, and their peers, who collectively build a substantial share of the world's AI servers without attaching a brand name to any of them. Quanta's Cloud Technology division supplies server platforms directly to Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon under each hyperscaler's internal hardware specifications. Wiwynn, majority-owned by Foxconn, grew into a dedicated AI server ODM with revenue in the billions, supplying Meta and other hyperscalers at scale. These ODMs compete in a structurally different lane from Super Micro entirely — their customer list is effectively the five largest cloud buyers in the world, their pricing reflects annually negotiated volume contracts, their margins are commensurately thin, and their differentiation lies in manufacturing scale and supply-chain integration rather than platform engineering velocity.

A hyperscaler that wants one hundred thousand servers built to bespoke rack specifications over eighteen months will typically go to a Quanta or a Wiwynn. A hyperscaler that needs the fastest path to Nvidia's latest platform in configurations already validated at production scale will frequently also engage Super Micro. That overlap defines the competitive tension — and the ceiling — of Super Micro's hyperscaler ambitions. Several large cloud customers had, by 2024 and 2025, moved toward direct ODM relationships for their highest-volume standardized GPU clusters while maintaining Super Micro relationships for specialized configurations and rapid new-platform deployments. Super Micro's hyperscaler revenue concentration — disclosed in aggregate in its SEC filings without naming specific customers — reflects this coexistence rather than clean displacement.

## The Modular Building Block Advantage

What separates Super Micro from every competitor is the Modular Building Block architecture — detailed in the IP & R&D chapter — in which chassis, backplanes, cooling, and power are interchangeable rather than integrated.

| Attribute | SMCI | Dell | HPE | Lenovo | Taiwan ODMs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary customer segment | AI cloud, hyperscaler, enterprise | Enterprise, government, hyperscaler | Enterprise, HPC, government | Enterprise, China domestic | Hyperscaler (direct) |
| AI server platform velocity | Fastest OEM | Moderate | Moderate | Slower | Custom / bespoke |
| Nvidia partnership depth | Deep (early HGX/MGX access) | Standard OEM | Standard OEM | Standard OEM | Direct ODM |
| Liquid cooling maturity | High (direct + immersion) | Growing | Growing | Growing | Customer-specified |
| Services/software margin layer | Minimal | Significant | Significant (GreenLake) | Moderate | None |

Super Micro's engineering teams work alongside Nvidia's solution architecture group during platform definition, before silicon tape-out, gaining access to thermal and power specifications earlier than competitors. That relationship enables a time-to-market advantage that had become one of the most-cited selection criteria among AI cloud customers.

None of these advantages are permanent. Dell's scale and enterprise relationships give it a durable position in regulated industries — financial services, healthcare, federal government — where procurement cycles favor incumbent vendors with full-stack service capabilities. HPE's Cray heritage and GreenLake platform anchor its position in national-laboratory HPC and large-enterprise services engagements. Lenovo's China domestic position is structurally insulated from Western competitive pressure. And the Taiwan ODMs, serving the customers who collectively account for the majority of global AI compute capital expenditure, will capture whatever share of hyperscaler AI server volume those customers elect to direct away from branded OEMs as they internalize hardware design further.

By the frozen snapshot date, Super Micro had demonstrated that speed, density, and thermal innovation could sustain a mid-market position between the ODMs and the conglomerates — differentiated enough to resist easy displacement.

chapters.title: From the FY2024 AI scaling through Hindenburg and special committee
chapters.body:
## A Franchise Built in Modules

Charles Liang's 1993 founding thesis — that configurability and speed-to-market win in servers — is detailed in the Corporate History chapter. The Modular Building Block Architecture became a decisive competitive weapon once the AI infrastructure cycle arrived. This chapter focuses on the major news catalysts from fiscal 2024 through 2025.

## The First Governance Crisis

The 2018 delisting and 2020 SEC settlement (detailed in the Corporate History chapter) prefigured the 2024 events. Liang remained as Chairman, CEO, and President throughout — the continuity of founder control meant no management break served as a visible governance reset.

## The AI Server Inflection

The FY2023-to-FY2024 revenue expansion — from $7.12 billion to $14.94 billion, a 110 percent year-over-year increase — places Super Micro's AI server scaling among the steepest in US enterprise hardware history. [Super Micro IR](https://ir.supermicro.com)

The driver was structural: hyperscaler and AI cloud operators were placing orders for Nvidia HGX-based GPU server clusters at volumes that compressed normal procurement lead times to weeks. The principal customers were hyperscaler cloud providers and a cohort of AI cloud companies — including CoreWeave, Lambda, Crusoe, and Nebius — that needed GPU clusters on compressed timelines. Super Micro's direct-liquid-cooling capability became particularly relevant as rack power densities climbed above the threshold where traditional air cooling becomes inadequate.

## August 27, 2024: The Hindenburg Report

On August 27, 2024, Hindenburg Research published a short-seller report on Super Micro Computer, alleging accounting manipulation, undisclosed related-party transactions, and export control compliance failures. Hindenburg, whose research targets had included Nikola, Adani Group, and Icahn Enterprises among others, presented its Super Micro report at a moment of maximum visibility — the AI infrastructure cycle was at peak investor attention, Super Micro's stock had appreciated roughly ninefold from its pre-cycle lows, and the 2018 accounting episode provided a historically plausible frame for fresh accounting concerns.

The market response was immediate. Super Micro shares declined sharply on the publication date as the allegations circulated through institutional investor networks. The company's public response was to deny the allegations, but the response was constrained by the structural fact that Super Micro had not yet filed its FY2024 annual report — the 10-K for the fiscal year ending June 2024 was overdue, a filing gap that independently elevated investor anxiety about the state of the company's financial reporting.

The Hindenburg episode illuminated a tension that runs through the Super Micro story: that Liang's concentrated control structure — Chairman, CEO, and President simultaneously, at a company where his co-founder wife Sara Liu also serves as Senior Vice President — provides exceptional operational agility and founder-grade strategic continuity, but creates governance opacity that short-sellers can credibly target when financial reporting timelines slip.

## October 2024: Ernst & Young Walks

The auditor resignation that followed made the Hindenburg allegations structurally more serious. In October 2024, Ernst & Young resigned as Super Micro's independent registered public accounting firm. The circumstances of the resignation — disclosed through a Form 8-K filing with the SEC — indicated that EY had become unwilling to be associated with management's representations, language that auditors employ only when concerns about financial reporting integrity have reached a threshold that professional standards do not permit them to simply waive. [SEC EDGAR, CIK 0000949486](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000949486)

The combination of a delayed 10-K, an active short-seller report, and a departing auditor produced the most acute governance crisis in Super Micro's history — worse, in investor perception terms, than the 2018 episode, because the scale of the company and the scale of the capital invested in the AI server cycle meant the systemic consequences of a genuine accounting failure were correspondingly larger.

NASDAQ issued a compliance notice. The possibility of a second delisting became a scenario that institutional holders were obligated to model.

## November 2024 Through February 2025: The BDO Restoration

The company's response moved on two parallel tracks.
